verdicts.trueWording: answers this question through a series of close readings
verdicts.note: Live page (analoggamestudies.org, browser UA). Sentence sits in the paragraph beginning 'Dread Trident's audience appears to be literary studies scholars'; page reads 'this question' (the book's stated secondary-focus question about gametexts and tools), which the claim renders as 'his question'. Quoted fragment appears word for word, and 'of several TRPGs' follows it on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Dread Trident's audience appears to be literary studies scholars
verdicts.note: Live page. Opens the paragraph on audience; quoted fragment is word for word, reviewer Adrianna Burton, dated January 9, 2022, matching the citation.

verdicts.trueWording: an overlooked area of investigation for literary scholars
verdicts.note: Live page (liverpooluniversitypress.blog). First answer, opening sentence, in Carbonell's own voice ('I was interested in how role-playing gametexts appeared to be...'). Note the source narrows the group with a following qualifier about fantasy and science fiction that the claim drops; no contradiction, but the claim is the broader statement.

verdicts.trueWording: I then began my close readings of the archives
verdicts.note: Live page. Closes the first answer's second paragraph. 'The archives' is unqualified in that sentence; the same sentence ends by locating the finding in the play of these gametexts, and the second answer supplies the forty years of published material, so the claim's gloss 'of published role-playing material' is carried by the page.

verdicts.trueWording: because of its simplicity or lack of textual and psychological depth
verdicts.note: Live page, second answer. The 'disputes' limb rests on the sentence's own structure: it is easy to say this, but that 'high-brow' critique holds less weight today when all manner of cultural activity is open to investigation.

verdicts.trueWording: forty years of published material was out there, waiting to be mined
verdicts.note: Live page, second answer, word for word. Two limbs are contextual rather than stated: 'role-playing' comes from the question being about TRPGs, and 'by a literary scholar' from the same sentence's opening, where Carbonell says he returned to it as an adult and literary scholar when he realised this. The page does not name a mining agent explicitly.

verdicts.trueWording: where we see literary tropes push up against game mechanics
verdicts.note: Live page, answer to the question on a standout TRPG. The sentence names D&D as exemplary for anyone interested in fantasy studies, then locates that 'middle ground' with the quoted words; both limbs on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: an impulse which Carbonell argues is also reflected in early TRPGs
verdicts.note: Live page (sfrareview.org), review signed Clare Wall, filed under 52.1, posted January 10, 2022. The preceding clause attributes to Lovecraft a materialism and impulse to categorize in rich description; the quoted fragment follows it word for word.
